title: MARV V2: Redesigning the Flight Computer
excerpt: What a season of flying MARV V1 taught me, how those lessons shaped the second revision of the flight computer, and how Rev 1 made it to manufacturing.

blocks.text: **Update, November 2026:** MARV V2 is final. Rev 1 is ordered and in production at JLCPCB. The final board and the manufacturing details are at the end of this post.

After flying MARV V1 through the IREC 2026 season, a handful of problems stood out. They spanned firmware, power and thermal design, and each one hurt performance or reliability enough that it had to be fixed in the next revision.

When I designed MARV V1, I didn't yet appreciate how critical data-ready interrupts are for real-time control. The firmware polled every sensor from one large loop, using a fairly involved retrieval scheme to pull samples from several sensors at once. It worked, but the code was complex and samples were often stale by the time they were read. As I kept working on the firmware, it became clear that if I wanted each sample the moment it was produced, the sensors had to signal the MCU through interrupts. MARV V2 uses data-ready interrupts, which removes both bottlenecks.

V1's onboard buck converter accepted 2S to 4S, so MARV always needed at least a 2S supply, even on telemetry-only flights. That complicated the coupler's power system: three of our four devices ran on 1S, but MARV needed 2S, so instead of a simple 4S pack we had to build an awkward 5S one. For V2, I moved the 5 V conversion off the board to an external power module, which can be chosen to fit each vehicle's power requirements instead of being tied to an onboard 2S–4S buck.

blocks.text: During the season, the AMS1117 LDO started overheating. Because it sat directly beneath the MCU, the heat was enough to shut the MCU down. We never pinned down why the problem surfaced so late, but my best explanation is that the sensors on the external I/O were drawing more current than the AMS1117 could handle. V2 replaces it with a 5 V to 3.3 V buck converter and gives the onboard sensors their own dedicated LDO.

items: **MCU power by the datasheet.** The RP2350 is particular about how its core-voltage regulator is set up, so V2 follows the datasheet's power routing closely.
**Single-sided assembly.** All components sit on one side of the board, which lowers manufacturing cost.

**Newer, rocketry-oriented sensors.** An ICM-45686 IMU on SPI0, an LSM6DSK320X secondary IMU with a ±320 g high-g channel on SPI1, and a BMP581 barometer on I2C1. Each sensor has its own bus, so no sensor ever waits on another one's traffic.
**Easier external I/O.** Standard 2.54 mm headers replace V1's small solder pads.
**4-bit SD card over PIO.** Higher SD throughput, SD traffic kept independent of sensor SPI traffic, and both hardware SPI controllers left free for the IMUs.

blocks.text: I simulated the power system in ngspice to confirm it works as intended, and bench testing for V2 is much more thorough than it was for V1. The goal is to catch sensor configuration mistakes before they're committed to the PCB.

blocks.text: While researching, I came across the FC3V2 on Tindie, a flight controller from madflight, a maker based in Switzerland. Its specs and design decisions are very close to MARV's, and it was reasonably priced, so I bought one to see what shortcomings a design this similar would run into.

blocks.text: After evaluating the FC3V2, I made a few changes to our board. I kept what worked well on MARV V1: the latching SD card slot, support for an external compass and GPS, and the ESC pad row. I left out the FC3V2's large via-stitched battery pads, since MARV won't connect directly to a battery in either of our setups. In the final design, power comes from a purchased 5 V converter module that plugs onto a three-pin header (J17), so the converter rides on the flight controller and the two mount as one unit. On a quadcopter, raw battery voltage comes in through the ESC pad row and feeds the converter, and USB-C can power the board on the bench. A boost module for 1S setups can use the same header, but it still needs fit and load testing. MARV V2 also keeps an optional QSPI footprint on the back for PSRAM: during firmware experiments, running the entire firmware from PSRAM instead of flash improved performance significantly.

blocks.text: Rev 1 is routed, checked and ordered. ERC is clean. DRC reports zero unconnected nets and zero schematic-to-PCB parity issues, and the few remaining DRC errors were reviewed and accepted. Most of them are the ground vias in the RP2354B's exposed pad, which follow JLCPCB's via-in-pad rule. The board sits inside a 72 × 72 mm manufacturing frame that gives the assembly line rails and fiducials to work with.

The order is five four-layer boards on 1.6 mm FR-4 with an ENIG finish, so the 0.4 mm-pitch QFN and the LGA sensors land on flat pads, and every board gets a flying-probe electrical test. JLCPCB assembles the surface-mount parts on the front side of two of them, and I'll solder the 2.54 mm headers myself. The repo keeps an order record with the exact upload files, their checksums and every option I selected, so Rev 1 can be reordered exactly.

blocks.text: Next is bring-up: power rails first, then each sensor bus in turn, then the firmware V2 was designed around, where every sensor sample arrives on a data-ready interrupt. The schematic, board, power simulations and design checks are open source in the [MARV-V2-PCB repository](https://github.com/Lmx154/MARV-V2-PCB). Thanks for reading, and I hope you found it useful!
